query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating, high-temperature sliding induces dynamic shear that refines the near-surface grain structure into an ultra-fine nanocrystalline layer; this microstructural transition shifts the dominant deformation mechanism from dislocation slip in coarse grains to grain-boundary–mediated sliding, which in turn enhances wear resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating with a relatively coarse grain structure on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Expose the coating to controlled high-temperature sliding (or a pre-conditioning thermal–mechanical treatment) designed to promote dynamic shear-induced grain refinement at the surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., operating temperatures in the range of 500°C to 700°C) and friction conditions typical for intended high-temperature applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-fine nanocrystalline (or dynamically amorphized) surface layer at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: The applied thermal and mechanical energy under high-temperature sliding promotes dynamic recovery and shear deformation, which refines surface grains. This shift leads to a transition from coarse-grained, dislocation-mediated plasticity to a smoother, grain-boundary–mediated deformation mode that suppresses the formation of highly localized defects and stress drops, thereby reducing wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline coarse-grained coating, the treated coating should exhibit lower wear rates and a more homogeneous microscopic deformation (e.g., fewer and less pronounced serrations in stress–strain curves) during high-temperature sliding.
generation.baseline: The wear and deformation behavior of the as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating (with its coarser grain structure) under similar high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: These predictions hold in the high-temperature regime where thermal activation enables significant dynamic grain refinement; they may not apply at lower temperatures or if substrate interactions dominate the deformation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact temperature threshold and shear conditions required to trigger the formation of the nanocrystalline layer, as well as the quantitative reduction in wear rate, remain to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical substrates. One set is maintained in the as-deposited state (baseline) and the other is subjected to controlled high-temperature sliding pre-conditioning designed to induce surface grain refinement. Then, perform identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (at, e.g., 600°C) while continuously recording friction and stress–strain responses. Following the tests, conduct detailed microstructural analysis (using TEM/SEM) of the worn surfaces to quantify grain size and deformation features.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., volumetric loss measured by profilometry)
Microstructural characterization (grain size, presence of ultra-fine surface layer via TEM/SEM)
Stress–strain curves to assess smoothness of deformation (e.g., absence of pronounced serrations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-conditioned coatings do not show a significantly refined near-surface microstructure compared to the baseline, or if no measurable improvement in wear resistance (i.e., similar wear rates and deformation behavior) is observed under high-temperature sliding, then the hypothesis that dynamic shear-induced grain refinement governs the improved wear resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
